sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Language is rich with lexical repetitions. Documents revisit entities and events, dialogues echo earlier turns, and code refers back to the same variables and functions. As result, 60% of the tokens in FineWeb-Edu (Lozhkov et al., 2024), popular pre-training corpus, already appear earlier in their 4k-token context. Copying from the context is therefore one of the most basic operations language model (LM) performs. Indeed, Transformer LMs devote many attention heads to copying, such as induction heads (Olsson et al., 2022) and retrieval heads (Wu et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026). Yet the standard neural LM setup can make copying surprisingly hard to learn. Every prediction is produced by the LM head, linear projection far narrower than the vocabulary. This low-rank layer limits the distributions model can express (Yang et al., 2018a; Finlayson et al., 2024), while also discarding most of the training signal before it reaches the backbone (Godey & Artzi, 2026). Copying is exposed to both effects, however easily the backbone can model the copy mechanism. As consequence, vanilla Transformer models fail on trivial synthetic copying task at large vocabulary sizes (Section 4.1). This raises the question of whether copying could be modeled more efficiently. Figure 1: Left: Our Copy-Paste (CP) head. The LM head uses the probability of special <copy> token to gate the copy distribution; special <sink> token allows rolling back to the LM head. The prediction mixes both heads. Right: FinePDF perplexity of our 1.7B models vs. memory footprint. CPLMs outperform their vanilla counterparts by 11.5 PPL, and the sliding-window (SW) CPLM matches full-attention LM at 12 less memory per token, copy cache included. 1 Pre-print. We introduce Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which are designed to facilitate copying in LMs. CPLMs are inspired by pointer networks (Vinyals et al., 2015), which were designed to give encoder-decoder and recurrent models direct access to their inputs, and largely fell out of favor with the emergence of self-attention. Yet we argue that key obstacle to copying lies on the output side, and that pointer offers way around the LM head bottleneck. CPLM adds Copy-Paste (CP) head adjacent to the LM head, which predicts the next token by pointing at past position in the context. The LM head decides when to copy by emitting dedicated <copy> token, and sink lets the CP head defer back to the LM head when nothing in the context is to be copied. This copy mechanism is learned directly in the vocabulary space, and adds second, much less compressed gradient pathway next to the LM head. Our contribution is thus not the adaptation of the copy mechanism itself, which is related to prior pointer models, but showing that such head substantially improves modern LM pretraining across backbones, and that it does so mostly by mitigating the LM head gradient bottleneck, as supported by targeted interventions (Section 4.1). The CP head adds two lightweight projection matrices and negligible parameter and compute overheads (resp. 0.5% and 3% at 1.7B scale, and below 1% of training throughput at 9B and 30B; Appendix B). Making copying easy to learn yields better models overall. We pretrain CPLMs from 135M to 1.7B parameters on up to 200B tokens across full-attention, sliding-window, hybrid and Gated DeltaNet backbones. CPLMs converge faster, reaching the final loss of their vanilla counterparts up to 2 faster, and improve perplexity at every scale and on every backbone, by 0.51.5 points on out-ofdistribution FinePDFs documents at 1.7B scale. These gains are not restricted to copied tokens: CPLMs also better predict the tokens they do not copy (Appendix G.1). Critically, the benefits carry over to supervised fine-tuning, where CPLMs improve on math, code and instruction following by 15 average accuracy points. CPLMs also change how models use their context. Sliding-window CPLMs match full-attention and hybrid models using up to 12 less memory per token, and they retrieve information from contexts far longer than those seen in training much better than their vanilla counterparts. CPLMs also rely on fewer induction heads in their backbone, suggesting that the CP head takes over part of their role. Moreover, the CP head can read documents through their copy keys alone, which offers memory-efficient alternative for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) setups. Finally, CPLMs demonstrate significant benefits even in extremely optimized environments: CPLMs improve on the prior NanoGPT speedrun (Jordan et al., 2024) record by 11.3%, achieving the largest architecture-centric speed-up and second largest overall since December 2024.

The LM head predicts the next token from ht, using learnable embedding wv RD for each token V. (1) Softmax Bottleneck(s) Commonly, the vocabulary size is much larger than the hidden dimension D. As all the logits ht are obtained from D-dimensional vector, the LM head cannot represent every distribution over V, which limits the model expressivity. This is commonly known as the softmax bottleneck, and has been shown to partly impede expressivity in practice (Yang et al., 2018a; Grivas et al., 2022; Finlayson et al., 2024; Basri & Jacobs, 2026). Godey & Artzi (2026) observe that the LM head also bottlenecks optimization by destructively compressing the - dimensional logit gradients to D-dimensional output space during the backward pass. sections.title: 3 EXPERIMENTS & RESULTS
sections.content: 3.1 PRETRAINING We pretrain models ranging from 135M to 1.7B parameters on up to 200B tokens of FineWeb-Edu data (Lozhkov et al., 2024). To study the interaction between backbone context handling and the CP head, we explore various backbones: full attention (Full), sliding-window (SW), and hybrid architecture (Hybrid) where full-attention and sliding-window layers are interleaved. Hybrid models give sliding-window backbones access to the whole context through few global layers, and thus serve as natural baseline for adding global access to local backbones, as for Sliding-Window CPLMs. Full and Hybrid backbones already access every position, so that CPLM gains on these backbones cannot stem from adding global access alone. We also report Gated DeltaNet (GDN; Yang et al., 2025) and Hybrid-GDN comparisons in Appendix C.5. At 135M scale, we run several ablations, notably varying the backbone sliding window for SW and Hybrid models, from 32 to 1,024. Based on our findings (Figure 3), we set = 256 for all Hybrid and SW 1.7B models. Our 61 135M-scale runs cost 50 GH200 hours each, and our 1.7B runs 900 B200 hours each. We follow the SmolLM2 recipe (Allal et al., 2025), with identical hyperparameters for both arms (Appendix A). All checkpoints are available on HuggingFace 2. We report our training dynamics for CPLMs and vanilla LMs at 135M and 1.7B scale in Figure 2, and at 360M scale in Appendix C.3. The dynamics are favorable to CPLMs in all configurations, reaching the final loss of vanilla models 1.25 faster in the Full and Hybrid attention setups, and 2 faster in the Sliding Window (SW) setup at 1.7B scale. The 1.7B SW CPLM matches the Full LM with 12 less memory at 4k tokens, as it only caches one copy key per token beyond its window. Ablations We conduct ablations at 135M scale to explore and validate several aspects of CPLMs (Appendix C). We run multi-seed analysis at 135M scale, showing that our gains are 1540 larger than the seed-to-seed standard deviation (p < 103), in line with the low sensitivity of pretraining loss to random seeds (van der Wal et al., 2025). We show that the dimension of the queries and keys in the CP head barely matters, with dimension 64 achieving similar performance to dimension 2,048, and that the sink matters most for small windows (Appendix C.4). Finally, we compare the CP head to alternative pointer designs (Appendix C.6): it outperforms the partitions that Chang et al. (2023) proposed for decoder LMs, and matches or outperforms sigmoid-gated (See et al., 2017) and shared-softmax (Gu et al., 2016) mixtures by small margins. 3.2 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING (SFT) We hypothesize that stronger token copying abilities result in better chain-of-thought reasoning and coding abilities, because copy is inherently important for these tasks. To validate this hypothesis, we perform Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on our pretrained 1.7B models. We use the Tulu-3 dataset (Lambert et al., 2025) with sequences of up to 16k tokens. Table 2 reports evaluation metrics for SFT 1.7B models. CPLMs outperform Vanilla LMs by 1.2 5.1 points in average score, and on every benchmark except MBPP for the Hybrid model. The Sliding Window CPLM is once again on par with full-attention models while using significantly less memory. The gap is particularly consistent on math benchmarks that benefit from chain-ofthought reasoning, and holds for every in pass@k (Figure 12). For mathematical tasks, CPLMs outperform their Vanilla baselines by +3.9 average points for full-attention models, and +7.9 for sliding window models. This downstream performance improvement is accompanied by the lower perplexity of CPLMs on both Tulu-3 and Nemotron-3 SFT data (NVIDIA et al., 2025), hinting that the CP head improves modeling for reasoning data. 6 Pre-print. 3.3 LONG-CONTEXT ABILITIES model that copies better is likely to also retrieve information more accurately from long documents. We verify this in Table 3, where we show that our base 1.7B CPLMs outperform their vanilla counterparts on both synthetic tasks (Hsieh et al., 2024; Kuratov et al., 2024) by +7.5 average points, and on LongBench (Bai et al., 2024) by +4.1 average points. We also run single-needle retrieval test. 7-digit magic number is placed at one of 8 depths inside neutral filler text, for context lengths from 1k to 64k tokens, i.e. up to 16 the pretraining context (details in Appendix E). Averaged over the whole depth/length grid, CPLM outperforms Vanilla for every architecture. The gain is small for Full attention (49.7 54.8), large for Hybrid 3:1 (58.2 83.6), and very large for SW (14.3 99.4). The SW CPLM finds the needle almost perfectly at every length and depth, with window of only = 256, showing that the CP head is robust to out-of-distribution context lengths, and can retrieve well beyond the sliding window. 3.4 EFFICIENT RETRIEVAL The CP head can be considered form of external memory. We study whether CPLMs can learn to copy from documents when the backbone has no access to the documents content. We fine-tune the base 1.7B vanilla models and CPLMs (Full attention, SW, and Hybrid 3:1) on the train set of HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018b) in the distractor setting. To enable robustness to variable number of distractor documents, each training sample contains the two gold paragraphs and U[5, 50] distractor paragraphs drawn from shared batch-level pool, with no context length truncation. All models are trained for one epoch, using learning rate of 104 with cosine decay, and batch size 32. We evaluate 200 validation questions with ranging from 5 to 500 distractors. We experiment with two regimes: (a) docs visible: the backbone attends over the whole input; and (b) docs dropped: each document is encoded independently by the backbone, so the question and answer tokens cannot attend to the documents in the backbone layers, but only reach them through the CP head. As control, we fine-tune vanilla baselines that we allow to reach the documents only through the lastlayer keys and values. All models are fine-tuned in their evaluation regime. CPLMs match or outperform their vanilla counterparts across backbones and distractor counts (Figure 5a) at small memory overhead: the CP head keys add 2% to the cache of full attention and 8% to Hybrid 3:1 (Figure 5c), and slow down decoding by less than 2% at this scale (Appendix B). The gap is largest with SW models, where the vanilla LM loses the documents that leave its window (15% EM at 20 distractors) while the SW CPLM still reaches 34% at 500 distractors, where every Full model fails. The CP head cache alone carries this retrieval ability (Figure 5b): with documents hidden from the backbone, CPLMs keep 9097% of their accuracy with 5 distractors and degrade gracefully as distractors grow, still reaching 3438% EM with 500 distractors, on par with or above every model that sees the documents in KV cache, while using 50 smaller cache than Full model. Since documents are encoded independently, their copy keys can also be computed once and reused across queries. In comparison, the last-layer control, with twice the memory of the CP head cache, stays at the level of model that never sees the documents (14% EM).

sections.title: 4 ANALYSIS
sections.content: 4.1 CPLMS MITIGATE THE LM HEAD BOTTLENECK Godey & Artzi (2026) show that the LM head unavoidably compresses the training signal when backpropagating it from -dimensional vocabulary space to D-dimensional hidden state space. They further show that the LM head loses as much signal as random matrix of the same shape: the compression level is essentially dictated by the ratio between and . As result, small models fail to learn simple patterns once the vocabulary is large compared to their hidden dimension, even when they should be expressive enough to model them. The CP head does not escape this random-matrix behavior, but its backward operator has much more favorable shape. At given sequence position t, the CP head query WQht goes through dotproduct with the CP head keys WKh1:t1, before softmax normalization. This is analogous to the LM head forward, where the CP head keys replace the output embeddings. However, the CP head 7 Pre-print. (a) Document KV (b) No Document KV (c) Memory requirements Figure 5: HotpotQA performance for 1.7B models. Models are fine-tuned and evaluated either with full document KV visible (left), or with only single access to the document memory: last-layer KV for Vanilla, and CP states for CPLMs (middle). logits are defined over the positions of the context rather than over the tokens of the vocabulary, so the CP head keys have shape instead of D. Since for typical contexts, the CP head logit gradient loses much smaller fraction of its norm than the LM head projection does, and this fraction depends on the sequence position rather than on the vocabulary size. We verify this using the experimental design of Godey & Artzi (2026), applied to CPLMs. Figure 6 (left) shows the fraction of the gradient norm lost in the LM head and in the CP head of our 135M Full vanilla model and CPLM, on FineWeb-Edu sequences of 2,048 tokens, and compare it to random matrix of the same shape as the CP head output matrix. The LM heads lose over 99% of the gradient norm, in line with Godey & Artzi (2026). Even if the compression level on the CP head keys pathway remains close to the random reference, their smaller shape lets them conserve up to 85% of the gradient norm at early positions. This opens much wider gradient channel than the LM head, especially at early positions. In Figure 6 (center and right), we additionally train 135M models using both architectures on the SpamLang synthetic task, where each sequence repeats single uniformly drawn symbol, with fixed hidden dimension (576) and vocabularies ranging from 8k to 512k tokens. As reported in Godey & Artzi (2026), vanilla models fail to reach strong performance for larger vocabularies (34% accuracy at 512k). CPLMs solve the task at every vocabulary size, showing that the CP head mitigates the LM head bottleneck in this setup. Further experiments validate that the benefits of CPLMs are tied to the LM head bottleneck (Appendix H). We conduct stop-gradient ablation, where we block gradients coming from the CP head to the backbone. This removes most of the benefits of the CP head, showing that backpropagating through the CP head pathway is crucial to the gains of CPLMs. We also pretrain byte-level language models, for which the softmax bottleneck is not active (D > = 257); we find that byte-level CPLMs do not improve on vanilla counterparts, hinting that the CP head is only helpful for bottlenecked setups. 4.2 CPLM BACKBONES LEARN FEWER INDUCTION HEADS Induction heads (Olsson et al., 2022) are attention heads that implement the simplest form of incontext copying: if the current token appeared earlier in the context followed by b, an induction head attends to that earlier and promotes it as the next token. They are central copying mechanism of Transformer-based language models. As the CP head performs this operation explicitly, we ask whether CPLM backbones still learn them. We use the probe of Olsson et al. (2022): sequence of uniformly random tokens, repeated once (T =2L). The first half is unpredictable, but every token of the second half can be predicted by copying from the first. We measure the NLL on the second half, and the induction score of each backbone attention head: its average attention from token of the second half to the token that followed its first occurrence. Heads scoring above 0.3 count as induction heads. 8 Pre-print. Figure 6: The CP head mitigates the LM head gradient bottleneck (Godey & Artzi, 2026). Overall, CPLMs have stronger copy abilities while exhibiting far fewer induction heads. CPLMs copy better with far fewer induction heads (Figure 7). Full and Hybrid CPLMs predict the repeated half almost perfectly at every length, while vanilla models degrade as the repeat distance grows. At =2048, the Full vanilla model is even worse than uniform guess (NLL 13.8 vs. ln =10.8), although the repeat lies within its training context. Meanwhile, CPLM backbones contain 4 induction heads at =128, against 1315 for vanilla models, and usually concentrate induction in single sharp head. The CP head thus takes over the copying work that vanilla models spread across many heads.

sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Softmax Bottleneck and Mitigations The low rank of the LM head limits the distributions an LM can express (Yang et al., 2018a). Usual remedies mix several LM heads (Yang et al., 2018a; 2019; Takase et al., 2018), or use element-wise non-linearities (Kanai et al., 2018; Ganea et al., 2019). How much this limitation matters in practice is debated (Grivas et al., 2022; Basri & Jacobs, 2026; Finlayson et al., 2024; Godey et al., 2024). These methods target forward expressivity and keep an output matrix shared across contexts, and therefore do not address the backward bottleneck of Godey & Artzi (2026), which the CP head mitigates with second gradient pathway (Section 4.1). Pointer and Copy Mechanisms The CP head is form of pointer network (Vinyals et al., 2015). Pointers have been combined with vocabulary softmax through supervised switch (Gulcehre et al., 2016), sigmoid gate (See et al., 2017), shared normalizer (Gu et al., 2016), or sentinel (Merity et al., 2017), mostly in encoder-decoder or recurrent models and to handle rare words. This line of work largely fell out of favor, as attention-based methods and most notably Transform9 Pre-print. ers (Vaswani et al., 2017) became dominant. In decoder-only Transformers, where self-attention can already retrieve any previous token, pointers are considered redundant. In line with our work, Chang et al. (2023) revisit pointer networks as remedy to the softmax bottleneck from the expressivity viewpoint. They partition the output softmax so that in-context tokens are scored by separate projections of the final hidden state, and continue training GPT-2, T5 and BART models with these heads. However, the LM head also bottlenecks optimization (Godey & Artzi, 2026): it compresses the signal that shapes the backbone during pretraining, which head added after pretraining cannot fully undo. Also, the CPR mechanism presented in Chang et al. (2023) does not use gating, and instead enforces copy when possible. In this setting, our <copy>- <sink> gating design outperforms their forced-copy approach (Appendix C.6). Externalized Memory The CP head is also context memory. The neural cache (Grave et al., 2017) and kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020) retrieve from past hidden states at inference, using them as form of external memory. We compare tuned neural cache to CPLMs in Appendix C.7, and show that neural caches bring no gain on our models. TRIME (Zhong et al., 2022) trains such cache jointly with the LM, mainly to exploit long-range and external memories at test time. Its localmemory variant is the closest prior model to CPLMs, but matches past contexts rather than pointing at past tokens, without gate or learned query and key projections. Zhong et al. (2022) also observe that local cache helps Transformers only when used during training, which the gradient-bottleneck view may explain (Section 4.1). Memorizing Transformers (Wu et al., 2022) attend to cached perlayer keys and values, RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022) cross-attends to retrieved chunks, CoG (Lan et al., 2023) copies phrases from corpus, and several RAG methods precompute per-document KV caches (Lu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025). Like the cache, the CP head stores one vector per token, but in dedicated learned key space. On HotpotQA, with documents hidden from the backbone, these keys alone keep 9097% of CPLM accuracy with 50 smaller total cache than full KV cache, whereas last-layer states with twice that memory fail (Section 3.4). The CP head also offsets the copying and recall weaknesses of sub-quadratic backbones (Jelassi et al., 2024; Arora et al., 2024): sliding-window CPLMs match full-attention vanilla LMs.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce Copy-Paste Language Models, which complement the LM head with lightweight pointer over past positions. Although self-attention can already retrieve any previous token, the copied token must still be decoded through the low-rank LM head, which affects copying abilities. Our CP head adds second, less compressed prediction and gradient pathway to circumvent the LM head bottleneck. At negligible cost, CPLMs train faster and improve perplexity, downstream performance, supervised fine-tuning and long-context results on every backbone we tested, notably enabling sliding-window models to match full attention with fraction of the memory. The CP head only relaxes the LM head bottleneck for tokens that appear in the context, and our experiments stop at 1.7B parameters. Extending the copy-paste mechanism to spans or to external corpora and studying how its benefits evolve at larger scales are natural next steps. All models are pretrained on FineWeb-Edu (Lozhkov et al., 2024), publicly available and filtered web corpus, fine-tuned on the publicly available Tulu-3 data (Lambert et al., 2025) and HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018b), and evaluated on public benchmarks. They are small research models that have not undergone safety alignment, and should not be deployed in user-facing applications without further evaluation. Because CPLMs copy from their context more easily, they may also reproduce sensitive or copyrighted content present in their inputs more faithfully. Conversely, sliding-window CPLMs reach the performance of full-attention models with much smaller memory footprint, which can lower the cost of inference.

sections.title: B LATENCY AND MEMORY
sections.content: The CP head adds two projections and sink key to the backbone, i.e. 0.5% more parameters at 1.7B and 9B, and 0.2% at 30B. The 9B and 30B models are untrained architectures, only used to measure time and memory. We measure what this costs in time and memory on single NVIDIA B300 GPU in bfloat16, comparing each CPLM with vanilla model with the same backbone. We focus on full-attention model for this analysis. Training. Table 5 reports training throughput and peak memory with sequences of 4,096 tokens. The CP head distribution and its contribution to the loss are computed with fused kernel, so that CPLMs never materialize the copy distribution over the vocabulary. At 1.7B, CPLMs train at 97% of the vanilla throughput, and the gap closes with scale: at 9B and 30B, the difference is within 1%, i.e. at the level of run-to-run variation. This is expected, as the cost of the CP head grows with the hidden dimension and the sequence length but not with depth, so that it becomes smaller share of each training step as models grow. Peak memory increases by 2.43.0 GB at 9B and 30B (1.72.6%). At 1.7B, computing this contribution over the 32k tokens of the batch at once adds 12.1 GB, and computing it in chunks of 8,192 positions reduces this overhead to 3.4 GB (+2.7%). 18 Pre-print. Ratio 1.096 1.026 1.017 Table 5: Training cost on one B300 GPU with sequences of 4,096 tokens. Ratios are CPLM values divided by vanilla values. At 1.7B, training step includes the AdamW update (batch of 8 sequences); at 9B and 30B, only the forward and backward passes fit on one GPU. Inference. At inference time, CPLMs cache one copy key per token, next to the keyvalue cache. During prefill, the copy keys of the prompt are written to this cache and the copy distribution is only computed for the last position, so that prefill never forms the copy scores. Each decoding step then adds single dot product between the copy query and each cached copy key, followed by the mixture with the LM head distribution. We measure generation with static cache, FlexAttention and decoding step compiled into CUDA graph, prefilling prompts of 4k or 16k tokens and greedily generating 256 tokens  (Table 6)  . Prefill time is unchanged: all differences are within 1.3% and go in both directions. decoding step is 1.03.8% slower. Since decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, the extra time is essentially that of reading the cached copy keys. It is largest when the keyvalue cache dominates the decoding step (large batches of long sequences), and smallest when reading the weights does (small batches). As prefill comes at no cost, the overhead per request is even smaller: for prompt of 4k to 16k tokens followed by 256 generated tokens, CPLMs add 0.81.7% to the total time. The copy cache holds values per token, against 2 nlayers nkv dhead for the keyvalue cache, i.e. 2.1% of the keyvalue cache at 1.7B and 6.2% at 9B, and decoding memory grows by exactly this amount. Remark on decoding cost. Our gate is token of the LM head, so the amount of copying is known before any copy attention is computed. Sampling can therefore proceed in two stages: sample from the LM head over {<copy>}, and only compute the copy attention when <copy> is sampled, falling back to pLM if the sink is then sampled. This is exact sampling from the mixture of Equation (7). For greedy decoding, copying adds at most λt ct to the probability of any token, while scaling the LM head distribution by 1 λt. Its average per length drops from 64 at 8k to 12 at 64k. With CPLM, 6084% accuracy per length remains from 16k to 64k, and the deeper needles are recovered best. The shallowest needles (d 2/7) are the hardest. Full. Both Full models fail completely from 16k on, even with YaRN. Retrieval does not generalize much beyond 2 the training length. CPLM helps in the transition region: at 8k, accuracy rises from 48 to 84, and Vanillas weak rows at shallow-to-middle depths are mostly recovered. CPLM does not move the failure point. In summary, CPLM helps most when the architecture cannot attend over the full context. When the backbones own attention fails beyond the window or past the training length, the CP head pathway keeps long-range retrieval working. LONG-CONTEXT EVALUATION Table 10 details the LongBench results of our base 1.7B models. The largest gains come from TREC, few-shot classification task where the answer labels can be copied from the in-context demonstrations: CPLMs improve it by +16.0, +29.0 and +24.5 points for Full, SW and Hybrid models, respectively. However, CPLMs also improve on tasks where copying is not crucial. On the three summarization tasks, whose outputs are abstractive, SW and Hybrid CPLMs improve over their vanilla counterparts on every task, by +3.6 to +6.2 points, although the Full CPLM is behind its vanilla counterpart on GovReport and QMSum. LongBench after SFT. Table 11 reports the same benchmark after supervised fine-tuning. CPLMs still improve the average score for every backbone (+0.6, +2.7 and +1.9 points for Full, SW and Hybrid models), but the gaps are smaller than for base models and less uniform across tasks. SW and Hybrid CPLMs keep large gains on TREC, while the Full CPLM is behind its vanilla counterpart on this task. Summarization gains are more consistent: CPLMs improve on GovReport and MultiNews for every backbone. Conversely, the SW CPLM loses ground on SAMSum and on code completion after fine-tuning. RULER and BABILong by context length. Table 12 extends the synthetic evaluations of Table 3 to 64k tokens. For Full and Hybrid models, CPLMs are better at almost every length up to 16k, and the Hybrid CPLM keeps an advantage on RULER at 32k. Beyond 16k, both Full models fail completely, which shows that the CP head does not compensate for the length generalization failure of the backbone. The SW CPLM improves RULER accuracy at every length, from 10.2 to 36.1 at 4k and from 5.0 to 18.9 at 64k, while both SW models remain close to the floor on BABILong beyond 2k tokens. Per-task results at 4k. Tables 13 and 14 break down RULER and BABILong at 4k tokens. For the SW CPLM, the RULER gain mostly comes from single-needle retrieval, which it solves almost perfectly (S1 and S2) while its vanilla counterpart cannot see beyond its window, and from word extraction tasks (CWE and FWE). For Full and Hybrid models, CPLMs improve on single and multi-key retrieval, multi-value retrieval and QA, but not on every task: the Full CPLM is behind on FWE and SQuAD, and the Hybrid CPLM on CWE and FWE. The hardest multi-key tasks (MK2 and MK3) remain near the floor for all models. On BABILong, the Full CPLM improves on all five tasks (18.6 32.6 on average), while the Hybrid CPLM is on par with its vanilla counterpart on average, and both SW models are close to the floor. 26 Pre-print. Figure 16 evaluates our 135M full-attention models on other languages, which are largely out of their training distribution. On English FineWeb, the CPLM improves perplexity by 0.3 points, i.e. about 2% in relative terms. On every other language, the gains are much larger, ranging from 14% (Arabic) to 22% (Mandarin Chinese) in relative terms, and reaching 4.4 points for Italian. This is in line with the larger gains observed on out-ofdistribution English data (Figure 3): when the model is less able to predict the next token from its parametric knowledge, copying tokens from the context becomes relatively more useful. 29 Pre-print. WHERE DOES THE GAIN COME FROM? In Section 4.1, we argue that CPLMs work mostly because the CP head provides gradient pathway that bypasses the LM head bottleneck. This section tests this argument mechanically, by removing each ingredient in turn. First, we keep the CP head as an output layer but remove its gradient benefits, by stopping its gradient into the backbone (Appendix H.1). Second, we keep the full CPLM but remove the LM head bottleneck itself, by training byte-level models whose vocabulary is smaller than their hidden dimension (Appendix H.2). If our argument holds, both interventions should remove most of the gains of CPLMs. All runs in this section use the 135M full-attention backbone and the training recipe of Table 4 (19,000 steps of 512 sequences of 2,048 units), with single seed. As in Figure 4, we report the mean copy probability ct and the mean sink probability st over validation positions. H.1 STOPPING THE COPY GRADIENT INTO THE BACKBONE Setup. In CPLM, the next-token loss reaches the backbone through two paths: the LM head, which also produces the copy gate ct through the <copy> token, and the CP head, through the queries qt = WQht, the keys kτ = WKhτ , and the sink score. We only cut the second path, by computing the queries and keys from detached copy of the hidden states: qt = WQ sg(ht), kτ = WK sg(hτ ), where sg is the stop-gradient operator. WQ, WK and the sink key are still trained with the full mixture loss of Equation (7), but they must now work with the representations that the backbone learns for the LM head. Everything else is identical to the CPLM. We verified that, with the stopgradient in place, loss computed from the CP head distribution alone sends no gradient into the backbone. Results. Stopping the gradient removes most of the benefit (Figure 17 and table 15). The CPLM improves on the vanilla model by 0.031 nats per token (0.49 PPL), against 0.008 nats (0.12 PPL) with the stop-gradient, i.e. about 25% of the full effect. This remaining gain is still several times larger than the seed-to-seed standard deviation of our main arms (0.0150.037 PPL, Appendix C.1): 30 Pre-print. the CP head alone, reading representations that were never shaped for it, gives small but real improvement. The dynamics of the gap are informative (Figure 17a). Early in training, the stop-gradient model is well ahead of the vanilla model (0.029 nats at 1B tokens): the CP head can already exploit easy repetitions that young backbone represents crudely. This advantage shrinks to about 0.010 nats by 5B tokens and to 0.008 nats at the end of training. The gap of the full CPLM starts larger (0.070), narrows to 0.040 at 5B and 0.035 at 10B tokens, and ends at 0.031 nats. The stopgradient model also uses the CP head much less (Figures 17b and 17c). Its copy probability falls from 0.18 after 250 steps to 0.046, against stable 0.21 for the CPLM, so that its effective gate λt = ct(1 st) is 0.036, against 0.091 for the CPLM. Its sink probability is also lower (0.22 vs. 0.57), as less copy mass needs to be routed back to the LM head. The model learns that CP head that it cannot shape is worth little, and mostly turns it off. Interpretation. Most of the gain of CPLMs comes from what the CP head gradient does to the backbone, rather than from the CP head as an additional output layer. CPLMs have no auxiliary loss: the backbone only receives the gradient of the next-token loss, but through two paths instead of one. The path through the CP head is much less compressed than the one through the LM head (Section 4.1), so that the backbone receives richer training signal, which in particular helps it represent the context features needed to copy, consistently with CPLM backbones needing fewer induction heads (Section 4.2). With the gradient path closed, WQ and WK can only linearly re-read features learned for the LM head, which are poor fit for position-level matching. This also explains why CPLMs improve the NLL of tokens that they do not copy (Appendix G.1): the backbone they share with the LM head is better trained. H.2 BYTE-LEVEL LANGUAGE MODELING Motivation. If the CP head mainly helped by escaping the LM head bottleneck, its benefits should vanish when there is no bottleneck. Byte-level models provide exactly this setting. Their vocabulary has = 257 entries (256 byte values and document separator, plus <copy> for CPLMs), fewer than the hidden dimension = 576. The LM head matrix RV then has full row rank: every distribution over the vocabulary can be expressed, and no component of the logit gradient is lost to the nullspace of , unlike for the token-level LM head of Figure 6. This setting is the limit of our SpamLang experiment (Section 4.1), where vanilla models only failed once the vocabulary became large compared to the hidden dimension. Setup. We train three byte-level models on the same data stream as our token-level models: vanilla model, CPLM, and CPLM without the sink. Each block of SmolLM2 tokens is decoded back to its raw UTF-8 bytes, which is lossless for byte-level BPE, and the first 2,049 bytes are kept as the training sequence, with byte mapped to id + 1 and the document separator to id 0. The backbone, sequence length (2,048, now in bytes), batch size, optimizer and schedule are unchanged, so that each model sees about 20B bytes, i.e. about 5B tokens worth of text. Only the embedding and LM head shrink, for about 107M parameters in total. Losses are in nats per byte. Val. Results. At the byte level, the CP head brings no gain (Figure 18 and table 16). Both CPLMs end within 0.002 nats per byte of the vanilla model (+0.0010 with the sink and +0.0016 without), which is comparable to the seed-to-seed standard deviation of our token-level models (Appendix C.1), and the training curves closely track each other throughout training. As for small backbone windows (Appendix C.4), the sink helps early in training (+0.0025 vs. +0.0096 nats at 1B bytes), consistent with its role as fallback while the CP head is still unreliable, but neither variant is ever meaningfully ahead of the vanilla model. 31 Pre-print. All three models reach the same loss within 0.002 nats per byte, even though the CPLM keeps high copy probability throughout training. The CP head is not idle, however. The CPLM keeps copy probability of about 0.34 throughout training, more than at the token level, and relies heavily on the sink (st 0.68), which leaves an effective gate of 0.11, comparable to the 0.09 of the token-level CPLM. Without the sink, the copy probability settles at 0.18. In both cases, the model copies at least as much as at the token level, yet its loss does not improve: bytes repeat constantly, so copying is easy, but full-rank LM head predicts them just as well. Interpretation. The byte-level results support the view that the token-level gains of CPLMs are tied to the LM head bottleneck. Once the LM head is full-rank and gradients reach the backbone without loss, pointing at the context gives the model nothing that it cannot express through the LM head. Together with the stop-gradient ablation, this draws consistent picture: with large vocabulary, the next-token loss reaches the backbone through the CP head as an additional training signal, bypassing the low-rank LM head (Section 4.1). This signal accounts for most of the gains of CPLMs, and it has nothing left to contribute once the LM head is no longer bottleneck. Both interventions thus remove most of the gains of CPLMs, as predicted by our argument in Section 4.1.
